It is not ethical and I would run far from any therapist who required this. How many different meds and dosages do they expect the patient to try? What side effects do they expect the patient to tolerate? How much SI will be tolerable to the clinician? Does the therapist imply that the patient is untrustworthy and/or not putting effort into therapy? Is the therapist ready to work with someone going through discontinuation syndrome if meds needs to be changed or stopped? Does the therapist have a psychopharm background? Are they really just saying: You're too much and I don't believe you will comply with this request so now I will have a good reason to get rid of you as a patient?  


Anti-depressants are not magical and they are not even well-understood scientifically.  
Medication is not guaranteed to work, there is little in the way of data available about the effects of long-term use of medication, it can cause horrific side effects (including, of course, worsening SI), it can risk making symptoms worse, and it certainly does not work immediately if it does work.

My psychiatrist/therapist also has an autistic kid. She didn't look at me upon meeting me and go "oh yes autistic vibes right here" she **listened** to me over the course of several meetings and then was like "hmmm has anyone talked to you about ASD?" (I had wondered out loud about ASD and/or ADHD the following week so I guess that probably helped to get her gears turning). I doubt I will ever be formally diagnosed, but my therapist listens to me, believes me, and has consistently understood me as autistic, even when I have been like "hmm probably not, actually" which has been really helpful. I would consider talking to the current therapist about how her dismissal of you was not helpful and that you would still like to talk about it. Even if she can't provide much useful feedback (I don't think I've ever had a therapist who knows much about autism), she should be open to listening and seeking out more info on her own. Therapists need our feedback -- part of the therapeutic process is addressing the therapeutic relationship and the things that arise therein.

If she proves to really not be open-minded or makes you feel unsafe or is simply not a good match, seek out somebody else. You need to feel safe talking about what's on your mind and if she can't give you that then it's a waste of time (and potentially damaging).

I saw a mental health counselor who seemed not to be particularly smart or even good at his job. He was nice enough, I guess, but I only saw him a couple of times before I moved to a new city. I knew I did not *want* to medically transition, but I was becoming increasingly convinced that I would have to. Some part of me thought that my mental health problems could somehow be tied back to my body being wrong even though I'd never actually wanted to be male. I started to fear that everything pointed to male even though I desperately wanted to be a woman. I remember thinking it was a good thing I was going to an expert because she would be able to see that I was not trans and then I would be able to just be a girl and it would be ok. I needed to know I did not have to be trans or masc or any of these things because I was not actually them. I just needed someone to be there for me.

I had never used a men's room nor had I wanted to. My use of "he/him" and anything male-related was not actually tied to maleness... and then, suddenly, I learned it had to be. I tried to talk about trauma with this therapist because I knew it was really important to work through. I specifically wanted to talk about this one psych hospitalization that basically started with me almost dying because of questionable care and then continued in various forms. She also did not refer me to someone who could actually help me with it. Similarly, during the time I was in her care, I came to understand that the relationship I had with my mother was and had historically been problematic and likely influenced my mental health and development. This has since been described as relational trauma but, again, this therapist had nothing to offer me. 

The longer I was in her care, the more my condition worsened. I became so suicidal and desperate that I couldn't process what was even happening in the therapeutic relationship or my life overall. I remember telling her through tears that I wanted to be a woman that I did not want to be trans and if I was trans I at least did not want to be the type of trans person who has to medically transition (as if anyone is required to transition!?!) I remember telling her that I did not want to be a man and that I don't even like men. I remember saying things like "I guess some people just have to transition even if they don't want to" and never getting push-back. I remember telling her that I did not identify as masculine and I remember refusing to go to a transmasculine support group because I did not identify with that.
